extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math instructors, and students evaluating or writing short proof write-ups (metric/topology context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and reader-reported criteria for judging short mathematical proofs (examples from metric-space problems), focusing on clarity and style for a student/teaching audience. Emphasizes notation, signposting, level-of-detail, and audience-awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: State what is to be proved (WTS / context-first)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin proofs by stating clearly what is to be shown (WTS) or otherwise give the context/goal up front so the reader knows the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commenters prefer an initial 'what to show' statement: 'I generally favour write-ups which begin by pointing out what it is that needs to be proved.' Anti-pattern: diving into manipulations and only announcing 'We've proved that...' at the end, which can surprise the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signpost strategy / give an outline of strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a short outline of the proof strategy so readers can see the big picture and know why steps are taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred for student-facing proofs: 'I prefer short outlines of strategy' and 'this declaration is useful, because it sketches the direction of the proof and gives students a path to guide their thoughts.' Avoid long sequences of details with no map.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor level of detail to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the amount of detail (low-level algebra/triangle inequality steps, reminders of definitions) depending on whether the audience is novice students or experienced readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters note different expectations: leave routine steps to reader for experienced audiences ('leaving out low-level details that the reader should be able to supply') but include reminders and explicit definitions for novices. State intended audience where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity vs completeness balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer concise presentation that omits mechanical details while preserving the idea; excessive verbosity can obscure the core idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many prefer concise proofs ('I personally like proofs where the ideas are presented concisely while carrying out the correctness is left to the reader') but caution that too terse proofs may not teach weaker students. Anti-pattern: overly long, repetitive proofs that delay the key insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce variables before use; avoid implicit quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Always introduce and name variables before making claims about them; avoid statements like 'y in A whenever d(x,y)<eta' without prior definition of y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple comments object to implicit quantification and letters introduced out of order: 'I don't like implicit quantification of the form "we know that y in A whenever d(x,y) < eta".' Teach students to introduce letters explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation consistency (balls, radii, variable roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use consistent notation for the same mathematical objects (e.g., B_r(x) vs B_x(r)); keep radii and centres clearly matched and use consistent letter-case to indicate different types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many dock style/clarity points for inconsistent ball notation or mixing small/large letters for radii: 'two inconsistent notations for balls are used' and 'the fact that a capital ‘R’ was used for the smaller radius ... irritated me.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intuitive / geometric language when helpful (open balls)
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, use open-ball language and geometric intuition (B_r(x)) rather than repeated metric inequalities, to make arguments clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several readers found ball-based arguments easier to parse than distance-based metric manipulations: 'I appreciated the style of stating what is to be done... The argument with balls is much easier for me to parse.' But also note audience: novices may need definitions of balls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary symbol proliferation
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the number of distinct symbols low; avoid introducing extra primes, unused variables, or multiple names for the same quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticized patterns: too many primes (x' , y' ), greek letters for numbers when not needed, or introducing u and v that are never used. 'There are too many symbols' and 'introducing yet a third name' reduces clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make key choices and definitions timely (avoid late crucial choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not postpone a crucial choice (e.g., setting a parameter) until the end of the proof without signposting; if you set a parameter at the end, explain why that completes the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers disliked constructions where a choice is made at the end forcing backtracking: 'The setting delta = theta ... forcing me to backtrack to understand why that completes the proof.' Prefer making the choice earlier or clearly saying why it's valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why steps achieve the goal (explicit linking)
rubrics_metrics.description: After manipulations, explicitly state how they imply the desired conclusion (e.g., 'By the definition of f^{-1}(U), f(x) in U'), not just 'so f(x) in U'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment: 'I would like "By the definition of the set f^{-1}(U), we know f(x) in U."' Helps weaker students see where definitions are used. Anti-pattern: leaving the reader to infer the final link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague endings like 'we are done' — state what was done
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude proofs by explicitly restating the achieved result and why it matches the target, rather than terse 'we're done' phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "The statement 'we are done' feels extremely unpleasant. It would be nicer to state what is done, and why." Make the concluding implication explicit for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer context-first ordering (Gopen's advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt 'context first' organization: present the goal/context before detailed steps, following principles from scientific writing research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referencing Gopen and 'context first', commenters recommend stating context/goal at the outset so readers do not have to reread to find what is being proved: 'context is stated first' gets positive marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear, mnemonic variable naming to indicate spaces/roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose variable names (lowercase/uppercase, subscripts) to signal the domain/codomain or role of a variable, helping readers track where each symbol 'lives'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: matching lowercase to uppercase to show 'where the variables live' praised; confusing choices (using 'a' as both limit and element) criticized: 'it’s extremely confusing that a and b are not elements of A and B, but are real numbers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid starting sentences with mathematical symbols in formal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: In textbooks and papers, avoid beginning sentences with bare symbols; in lectures or informal contexts this is more acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One commenter: 'I really dislike sentences which begin with mathematical symbols in textbooks or papers ... but I’m more relaxed about it in lectures.' Adjust to medium and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about assumptions and domain constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: State assumptions needed for steps (e.g., that a sequence is in A before concluding limit is in A) rather than implying them implicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism when proofs don't say why a limit belongs to A: 'Needed to know that Cauchy sequences imply completeness' and 'It would be good to say that because A is closed the limit of this x-sequence must be in A.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer balanced expressions and symmetric notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Write metric expressions and compositions in visually balanced forms to make relationships and symmetry clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example guidance: prefer d(f(g(x)), f(g(y))) over d(f(g(h(x))), z) — 'balanced expressions inside the metric' improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing notational conventions mid-proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not switch back and forth between two equivalent notations (e.g., metric inequalities vs ball notation) unnecessarily; stick to one clear style unless signposted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching reduces clarity: 'proof 2(b) starts with open balls, switches to metrics, then returns to open balls' was said to 'muddy the waters.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use meaningful punctuation and connectors (vary 'so', 'hence', 'therefore')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid repetitive use of a single connector (particularly 'so'); vary words and use punctuation to clarify logical relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers complained of many 'so's in succession: 'the word “so” is used too often ... relieve the tedium.' Vary transitions to aid flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide justification labels when using definitions (draw attention to definitions used)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a step depends directly on a definition (e.g., of continuity or inverse image), explicitly cite or reference the definition as justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters liked lines that say 'Since A is a closed subset of X, it must contain all its limit points.' Pointing to definitions/theorems helps learning readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary verbal clutter and redundant re-naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reintroduce the same object under different names or add superfluous verbiage that doesn't aid understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticized: naming the same common value with a third symbol or redundant restatement. 'This proof has more verbiage that doesn’t help clarify ...' Keep naming minimal and consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explicit set-theoretic wording where helpful (subset/member statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving set inclusions or membership arguments, state explicitly 'So P is a subset of Q' or 'an arbitrary element of P is an element of Q' to make the logical target explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment: 'I like a proof to say at the end, "So P is a subset of Q."' This makes the goal visible and is a useful teaching habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with choice of Greek vs Latin letters and their conventional uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use symbols in conventional ways (e.g., theta often for angles) and avoid introducing greek letters for quantities where latin would be clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One commenter: 'I see no need to use Greek letters when English ones will do fine. Theta, in particular, is typically used more for angles.' Choose symbols to minimize confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: State why particular numerical constructions (min, smaller radius) are chosen
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting constructions like 'take the smaller of two radii', explain the reason so the reader sees the logical role of the choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several readers wanted intuition: 'There’s a reason why it makes sense to consider the smaller of two particular radii ... proofs would be better if they explicitly dealt with the intuition behind the arguments.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal intended register (teaching vs research) and adapt style
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear whether the proof is pedagogical (for students) or terse/research-oriented; choices about signposting, verbosity, and notation depend on that register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark Meckes: 'I’ve judged the write-ups with my own undergraduate students in mind ... if you’re writing for colleagues I'd revise comments significantly.' Explicitly state audience to set expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple, readable function-composition notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use composition notation that is easiest to read in context; g(f(x)) is often clearer than circle notation g∘f or other multiline forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple readers prefer g(f(x)) over composition-circle: 'I prefer (g∘f)(x) for function composition, or better yet, g(f(x)), as in the 4(c) proof.' Choose notation that reduces parsing effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid careless typographical errors and misprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Typos in notation (e.g., B_r(x) vs B_x(r), or wrong references) harm perceived quality and can confuse readers; correct them or clarify if intentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several readers flagged apparent misprints and deducted style points: 'is that an intentional misprint?' 'Where it should be B_r(x) not B_x(r).' Proofs should use correct, consistent typography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit when using existence statements (use 'there exists' rather than ambiguous phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using existential quantification, use clear phrasing ('there exists', 'let r>0 be') to avoid ambiguity whether a value is arbitrary or uniquely chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: 'It was unclear at first that r and r’ could be arbitrary rather than the smallest or largest such values; "there exist" would have been more familiar.' Use explicit existential language.
